The Mauritius fody (Foudia rubra) is a critically endangered passerine endemic to the island of Mauritius, where it inhabits remnants of native upland forest. Field studies on this weaver finch have provided a detailed picture of its life-history strategy, which is shaped by the constraints of a fluctuating tropical environment. Eggs artificially incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days], an incubation period comparable to that of other ploceids of similar body size. The newly hatched altricial nestling is remarkably small, with a recorded wet weight at birth of just 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams], representing a tiny fraction of the adult mass. This minimal neonatal investment reflects a reproductive strategy centred on rapid post-hatching development under the sustained provisioning of both parents. The initial vulnerability of the chick, which relies entirely on parental care for thermoregulation and feeding, imposes a significant energetic burden on the breeding pair, particularly during the early nestling phase when the brood is most susceptible to predation and adverse weather.

As the nestling develops, it undergoes a period of rapid somatic growth that culminates in the achievement of flight. Under the typical body temperatures of an active brooding adult, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging, defined as the time since birth at which the young bird departs the nest, occurs at approximately 14.27 days [tx = approximately 14.27 days]. This remarkably short nestling period is an adaptation to the high predation pressure typical of island ecosystems, where nests are vulnerable to introduced mammalian predators such as rats and monkeys. The fledgling, though capable of short flights, remains dependent on its parents for several weeks thereafter, gradually improving its foraging skills. The rapid transition from a 1.5-gram neonate (1.5 grams) [Wwb = 1.5 grams] to a fully feathered juvenile capable of leaving the nest underscores the intensity of parental food delivery during the brooding phase. Growth rates during this period are among the highest recorded for any ploceid of comparable adult dimensions.

Sexual maturation in the Mauritius fody proceeds steadily after independence, though it does not coincide with the onset of breeding activity. Under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterises the active metabolic state of this species, puberty is attained at 42.81 days since birth [tp = 42.81 days since birth]. This marks the physiological point at which the gonads become capable of producing gametes, yet the young bird typically does not breed until considerably later. The delay between physiological maturity and first reproduction is a common life-history feature among tropical passerines and is thought to be related to the time required for a young bird to acquire a high-quality territory and develop the foraging proficiency necessary to support a clutch. First-year birds often remain as non-breeding floaters or join small flocks, postponing reproductive investment until their second year of life when they can secure a nesting site in the increasingly fragmented forest patches of the island.

The age at which a Mauritius fody initiates its first reproductive attempt is considerably later than the attainment of puberty, reflecting the substantial ecological hurdles faced by young birds. First brood production typically occurs at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], a full year after hatching, under the metabolic conditions associated with a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This extended delay is attributed to the species' need to navigate a complex social structure and compete for limited nesting resources in degraded habitat. Once a bird successfully establishes itself, it may attempt to rear one or two broods per breeding season. The species is generally monogamous for the duration of a breeding attempt, and both parents invest heavily in nest construction, incubation, and chick rearing. Females produce either one or two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one or two eggs per clutch], and the available evidence suggests they raise approximately two to four broods per year [F_R_i = approximately two to four broods per year] given the challenges posed by nest predation and inclement weather.

Longevity data for the Mauritius fody are limited, but comparative estimates based on the closely related house sparrow (Passer domesticus) offer a useful reference for maximum lifespan. Under the thermal conditions of an endothermic passerine operating at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the total lifespan is projected to be on the order of 8395 days [am = 8395 days]. Whether any individual in the wild attains this theoretical maximum remains uncertain, as field records suggest high annual mortality among adults, driven primarily by cyclones and introduced predators. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult Mauritius fody is approximately 17 grams [Wwi = approximately 17 grams], a value consistent with the species' placement among the smaller ploceids. This modest adult body mass means that even small fluctuations in food availability — such as reductions in arthropod prey following heavy rains — can quickly impact body condition and reproductive output. Conservation efforts focusing on habitat restoration and predator control remain essential for the persistence of this endemic island specialist.
